text: The Argentine general election of 1989 was held on 14 May 1989, with voters selecting both the President and their legislators; the turnout was 85.3%. Carlos Menem won the presidency, and the Peronist Justicialist Party secured control of both houses of Congress. This was the last presidential election in which the president was elected by the electoral college. President Raúl Alfonsín, representing the Radical Civic Union (UCR), inherited a difficult legacy from military dictators, primarily due to Argentina's massive foreign debt. His 1985 Austral Plan for economic stabilization failed, leading to a loss of support for the UCR, which lost its majorities in the Chamber of Deputies and in 22 governorships during the September 1987 mid-term elections. Facing an armed forces opposed to trials for past human rights abuses and rising inflation, Alfonsín brought elections forward five months, setting them for May 14, 1989. Both major parties held national conventions in May 1988; the UCR nominated Córdoba Governor Eduardo Angeloz, a centrist figure not closely tied to Alfonsín, while the Justicialist Party nominated Carlos Menem, governor of La Rioja, who defeated the favored candidate, Buenos Aires Governor Antonio Cafiero, a close ally of Juan Perón. Cafiero's defeat stemmed largely from opposition by the CGT trade union to his Peronist Renewal faction, and Alfonsín's top adviser, Interior Minister Enrique Nosiglia, viewed Menem's flamboyance as a strategic opportunity for the struggling UCR. Early polling showed the Justicialists leading, with nearly half of voters undecided. In response, Alfonsín introduced an August 1988 "Springtime Plan" to reduce inflation (then at 27% monthly), which included budget cuts and renewed wage freezes—measures criticized by the CGT as a rehash of the Austral Plan and blamed for declining living standards. Though initially successful, a severe drought late in the year damaged export revenues and caused rolling blackouts, undermining any gains Angeloz might have achieved from the 6% monthly inflation reduction. Conservative economist Álvaro Alsogaray, a perennial third-party candidate, gained traction after the January 1989 attack on the La Tablada Barracks by Trotskyist militants. Alsogaray, a former minister of economy who believed in an economic "winter," ran on a free-market platform advocating mass privatizations and deep cuts in social spending amid 30% poverty. Angeloz included social spending cuts in the UCR platform, earning the endorsement of the right-wing Federal Party but alienating many, especially pensioners, whom Alfonsín had won in 1983. The campaign became increasingly focused on the debate between Menem and Alfonsín, with Angeloz remaining a "presidential" figure amid frequent exchanges of innuendo. On "black Tuesday," February 7, Central Bank reserves dropped sharply, causing the austral to fall 29% against the U.S. dollar. The World Bank recalled a major loan from 1988 later that month, plunging the austral into a tailspin: trading at 17 to the dollar in January, it reached over 100 australes by election day. Inflation, which had stabilized at 5–10% monthly by February, surged to 78.5% in May, breaking records and resulting in a Peronist landslide. Polling indicated that economic concerns were central to two-thirds of voters, and Menem won in 19 of 22 provinces, losing only in the traditionally anti-Peronist Federal District (Buenos Aires). Despite hopes for financial stabilization after the election, the austral halved to the dollar the following week, and on May 29, riots erupted in poorer urban areas. Having declared his intention to remain in office until December 10, Alfonsín transferred power to President-elect Menem five months early on July 8 due to escalating financial chaos and public unrest. When Menem accepted the presidential sash from Alfonsín, it marked the first peaceful transfer of power from an incumbent to the opposition since 1916.
